clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder of DNA repair, caused by variants in nucleotide excision repair genes (complementation groups XPA-XPG) or in POLH (XP variant)
Defective repair of ultraviolet-induced DNA damage causes extreme photosensitivity and a very high risk of skin cancers at a young age
Early signs include severe sunburn from minimal exposure and, later, freckling and poikilodermatous change on sun-exposed skin in early childhood
Cutaneous squamous and basal cell carcinomas and melanoma arise decades earlier than in the general population
Ocular involvement is prominent: photophobia, conjunctivitis, keratitis, and periocular tumours
Some complementation groups develop progressive neurological degeneration (the neurological form)
Rigorous, lifelong photoprotection and surveillance are the cornerstone of management
reference.pathophysiology: Xeroderma pigmentosum is caused by inherited defects in the nucleotide excision repair pathway, which normally recognises and removes bulky DNA lesions such as the cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers produced by ultraviolet radiation; the XP variant form instead reflects loss of DNA polymerase eta, needed for accurate translesion synthesis. Because damaged DNA cannot be repaired efficiently, ultraviolet-induced mutations accumulate in keratinocytes, melanocytes, and ocular surface cells. This drives premature photoageing, pigmentary change, and early malignant transformation. In certain genotypes, accumulated unrepaired damage in neurons produces progressive neurodegeneration independent of sun exposure.
additionalDifferentials: Polymorphic light eruption and other photodermatoses
Cockayne syndrome and trichothiodystrophy (related repair disorders)
Rothmund-Thomson syndrome and Bloom syndrome (photosensitive genodermatoses)
Carney complex or familial multiple naevi in early skin cancer presentations
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of XP complementation group genes and POLH
Cellular assays of DNA repair capacity (unscheduled DNA synthesis) where available
Skin biopsy of suspicious lesions for early tumour detection
Regular full-skin and ophthalmological surveillance examinations
Neurological assessment (including audiometry) in genotypes prone to degeneration
Ultraviolet exposure and minimal erythema history to gauge photosensitivity
redFlags: New, changing, or non-healing skin lesion requiring urgent biopsy for malignancy
Ocular surface deterioration, corneal scarring, or periocular tumour
Progressive neurological decline (hearing loss, ataxia, cognitive regression)
Evidence of inadequate photoprotection with escalating actinic damage
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is reduced, largely from early and recurrent skin and ocular malignancies and, in neurological subtypes, from progressive neurodegeneration; with meticulous photoprotection and close cancer surveillance, tumour burden and its consequences can be substantially reduced.
pitfalls: Attributing childhood 'freckling' and severe sunburns to ordinary sun sensitivity and missing the diagnosis
Under-recognising the lifelong intensity of photoprotection required, including indoor ultraviolet sources
Neglecting ophthalmic and neurological surveillance in favour of skin monitoring alone
Delaying biopsy of new lesions given the accelerated pace of malignant change
management: Institute rigorous lifelong ultraviolet protection as the cornerstone of care: sun avoidance, protective clothing, UV-filtering eyewear and window films, broad-spectrum sunscreen and indoor UV shielding
Undertake frequent full-skin and ophthalmological surveillance to detect and excise cutaneous squamous and basal cell carcinomas, melanoma and ocular surface tumours early
Treat established skin malignancies with surgical excision, and consider oral retinoids as chemoprophylaxis in patients with a heavy tumour burden
Manage ocular surface disease with lubricants and protection against photokeratitis, referring for corneal or lid surgery when required
Supplement vitamin D, since strict sun avoidance predisposes to deficiency
Monitor genotypes prone to neurodegeneration with neurological review and audiometry, providing supportive and rehabilitative care
Offer genetic counselling and testing for the autosomal recessive nucleotide-excision-repair (XPA-XPG) or POLH variants, with carrier testing and reproductive options
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across dermatology, ophthalmology, clinical genetics, neurology and oncology, and avoid tobacco smoke and other DNA-damaging exposures
